overview: Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country in the Balkans. Its capital is Sarajevo. It was part of Yugoslavia until it declared independence in 1992, which was followed by a war that lasted until 1995. Today the country is made up of two main parts, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, plus the small Brčko District.

geography.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina is mostly mountainous, with the Dinaric Alps running from north-west to south-east. Bosnia, the larger northern part, has forests and river valleys, while Herzegovina in the south is drier, with bare limestone hills. The country reaches the Adriatic Sea along only a very short stretch of coast, at the town of Neum.

history.text: Medieval Bosnia was an independent kingdom until the Ottomans conquered it in the 1460s. Austria-Hungary took control in 1878, and in 1914 the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo set off the First World War. After decades in Yugoslavia, Bosnia's independence in 1992 was followed by a devastating war that ended with the Dayton Agreement in 1995.

events.title: Ottoman conquest
events.text: The Bosnian kingdom falls to the Ottoman Empire.

events.title: Assassination in Sarajevo
events.text: The killing of the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne triggers the First World War.

events.title: Winter Olympics
events.text: Sarajevo hosts the Winter Olympic Games.

events.title: Independence and war
events.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina declares independence and war breaks out.

events.title: Srebrenica and Dayton
events.text: More than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys are murdered at Srebrenica; in December the Dayton Agreement ends the war.

government.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina has one of the world's most complicated systems of government, set up by the Dayton Agreement in 1995. It is divided into two entities, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, plus the Brčko District. The presidency is shared by three members, one Bosniak, one Croat and one Serb, and an international High Representative oversees the peace deal.

economy.text: The economy was badly damaged by the war of the 1990s and has been rebuilding since. Industry includes metals, wood and furniture, and energy from coal and hydropower. Many young people move abroad for work, and money they send home is an important source of income.

culture.text: Bosnia sits where Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian worlds met, and its towns mix mosques, Orthodox and Catholic churches and synagogues. Sevdalinka is a style of emotional folk song. Ćevapi, small grilled sausages served in flatbread, are a national favourite.

items.title: Stari Most
items.text: The Old Bridge in Mostar, built by the Ottomans in 1566, destroyed in 1993 and rebuilt in 2004.

items.title: Sarajevo
items.text: A city where a mosque, a cathedral and a synagogue stand within a short walk of each other.

items.title: Ivo Andrić
items.text: Won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1961 for novels such as The Bridge on the Drina.

sport.text: Football is the most popular sport, and the national team reached the World Cup for the first time in 2014. Basketball and handball are also widely followed. Sarajevo hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics.

items.text: Sarajevo hosted the Winter Olympics, the first held in a communist country.
Bosnia and Herzegovina's first men's World Cup.

items.title: Bridge diving
items.text: Divers have jumped from Mostar's Old Bridge into the river for centuries.

didYouKnow: Sarajevo was one of the first cities in Europe to have a full-time electric tram network, in 1895.
Bosnia and Herzegovina has only about 20 km of coastline, at the town of Neum.
